LDA implementations in R and Python

Where tidylda sits in the ecosystem

What this measures

Ten LDA implementations, fit on identical document-term matrices with identical hyperparameters (alpha = 0.1, eta = 0.05, no hyperparameter optimization anywhere), scored by one common code path. Each run is its own OS process under /usr/bin/time -v.

Color encodes the algorithm family. Engine names are labeled directly on the curves.

Corpora
Corpus Documents Terms Tokens Mean doc length

1. Quality against wall-clock time

The headline result. A Gibbs sweep and a variational pass are different units of work, so comparing “200 iterations each” would compare two arbitrary numbers. Instead each engine is run at a ladder of iteration counts, single threaded, and we plot the quality it reached against how long it took. Down and to the right is worse; up and to the left is better. A curve that sits above and to the left of another dominates it.

2. Thread scaling

Only some engines thread at all. For those that do, this is speedup relative to their own single-threaded time — so it answers “does adding cores help this package”, not “which package is fastest” (that is the chart above).

Threading is not free of consequences for every engine. MALLET and tomotopy use parallel samplers that do not preserve the exact collapsed Gibbs chain; tidylda’s is documented to be invariant to thread count, and scripts/98-verify.R confirms its parameters are bit-identical at 1 and 20 threads. So it is worth checking whether quality moves as cores are added:

3. Memory

Peak resident set size of the whole process, so it includes the interpreter or JVM baseline. The baselines are shown rather than subtracted.
